technical.lead: Siri rebuilt from the ground up on a custom 1.2T-param Google Gemini model
technical.body: At its WWDC keynote on Monday June 8 - Tim Cook's last as CEO - Apple unveiled a Siri rebuilt from the ground up and powered not by Apple's own models but by a custom version of Google's Gemini: a roughly 1.2-trillion-parameter mixture-of-experts system, about eight times larger than the biggest cloud model Apple had built in-house, designated internally as "Apple Foundation Models v10." Apple frames privacy as topology - a roughly 3-billion-parameter on-device model handles local requests, and heavier work routes to Apple Silicon servers under Private Cloud Compute (stateless, ephemeral, with personally identifying information stripped before any content reaches the Gemini inference layer) rather than to Google's infrastructure. The user-visible result is a Siri that behaves like a full chatbot: a dedicated app, a system-wide "Search or Ask" gesture, Dynamic Island integration, on-screen awareness, personal-context retrieval, and multi-step actions chained across apps, with developer betas of iOS 27 and its siblings shipping now and a general release in the fall.

technical.lead: Apple pays Google about $1B a year to license its assistant's intelligence layer
technical.body: The economics behind the Siri rebuild are as striking as the technology. The multi-year arrangement to license a custom Gemini model is reported to cost Apple on the order of $1 billion a year, with analyst estimates of total value running up to $5 billion. After years of struggling to ship a competitive assistant, the iPhone maker has outsourced the intelligence layer of its flagship AI feature to the same company that already pays Apple to be the default search engine on its devices - a bet that owning two billion devices and the user gateway matters more than owning the best model. The licensed model is roughly eight times larger than the biggest cloud system Apple had built in-house, underscoring how far behind its own foundation-model efforts had fallen and why renting a rival's frontier model became the pragmatic path.

technical.lead: The system assistant becomes a user-selectable model slot
technical.body: iOS 27, iPadOS 27 and macOS 27 introduce an Extensions mechanism that lets users pick which assistant answers from the new "Search or Ask" panel - routing a query to Siri, Google Gemini, or ChatGPT, with Apple confirmed to have tested Anthropic's Claude as an additional option. For the first time this makes the system assistant a model-agnostic slot rather than a fixed Apple service: the assistant brain is selectable by the user instead of being permanently wired to one vendor. It is a notable reversal for a company that has historically controlled its default services tightly, and it reframes the iPhone's assistant layer as an open competitive surface where multiple model providers can be plugged in behind the same system-wide gesture.

technical.lead: App Intents plus a free on-device model turn the iPhone into an agent surface
technical.body: The developer-facing half of the announcement may matter more to the agent ecosystem than the Siri rebrand. Apple is deepening App Intents - the framework that lets Siri, Spotlight and Shortcuts invoke actions inside third-party apps - as the mechanism by which the new assistant chains tasks across apps, and pairing it with the Foundation Models framework that exposes the on-device model to developers for tool-calling and guided (structured) generation with no per-call charge, since the model runs locally. The practical takeaway for anyone building agentic features is that the largest consumer device base is becoming an addressable agent surface in two directions at once: apps can expose their capabilities as intents an assistant can orchestrate, and apps can call a free on-device LLM for structured output and tool use. The detailed API sessions run June 9-12, so how strict the entitlements and tool-permission model will be is still being filled in.

technical.lead: The summer AI-event calendar: WWDC now, then the security and chip tracks
technical.body: The still-upcoming AI calendar worth planning attendance around spans three tracks. On the mainstream developer side, Apple WWDC26 is underway, having opened June 8 and running through June 12; the Databricks Data + AI Summit follows June 15-18 at Moscone (30,000-plus in person, 800-plus sessions); and the AI Engineer World's Fair runs June 28-July 2 at Moscone West with 29 tracks including agentic, inference and security tracks. On the AI-security track, the Confidential Computing Summit lands June 23-24 at the San Francisco Mint with a schedule built around agent security and attested inference, SecurityWeek's AI Risk Summit follows August 11-12 at Half Moon Bay, and Black Hat USA's AI Summit (August 4) plus DEF CON 34's AI Village anchor the agentic red-teaming calendar, with Zenity's practitioner-led AI Agent Security Summit confirmed to expand to New York, London and APAC. On the AI-chip track, AMD's Advancing AI 2026 is slated for July to detail Instinct MI400 / MI455X availability, Hot Chips 2026 takes Stanford August 23-25, and the AI Infra Summit runs September 15-17 in Santa Clara.
